answer.rationale:
The strongest causal signal is temporal: the release went out 2h ago and write-path p99 began climbing 90m ago, which fits a post-deploy regression better than the alternatives. Capacity (b3) and failover (b2) do not address a defect that would travel with the traffic; a circuit breaker (b4) helps a failing external dependency, and there is no evidence of partner failure here — it would shed customer writes, directly violating the objective. So rollback is the leading candidate, but I want it verified rather than assumed.

I am verifying memory_b1 because it is the load-bearing memory and it may not say what I need it to say: it records a rollback clearing a checkout ERROR spike, not a write-path LATENCY climb, and it says the prior build was stable and the rollback was clean. Those are different failure modes and different preconditions. The archived record should tell me whether that rollback was performed under heavy write load and whether the release included schema or data migrations — a rollback across a migration during peak settlement is exactly how you lose customer writes, which is the one outcome the objective forbids. I am verifying memory_b5 because it is the best competing hypothesis for a write-latency symptom specifically (contention on the primary), and if the archive shows that case presented as a gradual p99 climb rather than a deploy-correlated step, my ranking should change; read-replica routing is also the cheaper, non-destructive move.

I am scoping this as a small guarded test: roll back one cell or a limited shard of write traffic and compare p99 against unrolled cells, per the canary logic in memory_b6, which showed cohort-level signal inside an hour. That converts a correlation into evidence before I spend the single intervention on a broad change during peak settlement. If the archived records show migration risk or point to primary contention, I will switch to route_read_replicas. Residual uncertainty is real: three things are confounded, the release-timing link is correlational, and every inherited memory describes a single-cause incident rather than a simultaneous one.
